entities.name: Pamplona Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Pamplona Cathedral (Cathedral of Santa María la Real de Pamplona) in Navarre, northern Spain — built in Gothic style between 1394-1501 CE on the site of a Romanesque cathedral destroyed by earthquake — is one of the finest Gothic cathedrals in Spain and the seat of the Archdiocese of Pamplona. The cathedral is particularly notable for its 14th-century Gothic cloister, considered one of the most beautiful Gothic cloisters in Europe and certainly the finest in Spain, with tracery and sculpture of exceptional delicacy.

Pamplona — the ancient Roman Pompaelo, the city made famous by Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises and the Running of the Bulls festival (San Fermín, July 6-14) — has been the capital of the Kingdom of Navarre, a historically strategic buffer kingdom between France and Spain that maintained its independence until 1512. The cathedral served as the burial place of the kings of Navarre including Charles III 'the Noble' (d. 1425) whose alabaster tomb, by Johan Lome de Tournai, is one of the masterpieces of late Gothic funerary sculpture in Europe.

The cathedral's 18th-century Neoclassical facade (by Ventura Rodríguez, 1783) contrasts with the Gothic interior, making Pamplona Cathedral an unusual fusion of Gothic and Neoclassical aesthetics. The cathedral stands on the pilgrimage route — Pamplona is one of the first major Camino de Santiago waypoints after entering Spain from France through the Pyrenees — giving it significance in the pilgrimage tradition alongside its role as Navarre's royal church.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pamplona Cathedral — royal burial church of Navarre's kings, home to Spain's finest Gothic cloister, containing one of late Gothic funerary sculpture's masterpieces, and a key Camino de Santiago waypoint — is a monument where Navarrese royal history, Gothic architecture, and pilgrimage tradition converge.
